question.problem:
We wish to construct a cylindrical can with a base and a lid. Our cylinder must have an exact volume of $128\pi \,{\text{ft}}^{3}.$ What is the smallest surface area we can get? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

$S=$
{{field-1}} ${\text{ft}}^{2}$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a picture of a cylinder. Let $r$ be the radius, and $h$ the height.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14195873/assets/bb9c356aadbb184aaa49c1fa1867da82d64ef40db9048c752c2a91d20704392a.png)

We wish to minimize the surface area

$$
S=2\pi rh+2\pi {r}^{2}.
$$

We know that the volume is fixed at $128\pi \,{\text{ft}}^{3},$ so we also have the constraint condition

$$
128\pi =\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
h=\frac{128}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $S,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S(r) & =2\pi r(\frac{128}{{r}^{2}})+2\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{256\pi }{r}+2\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to minimize $S,$ so we need to differentiate $S$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{S}^{′}(r)=-\frac{256\pi }{{r}^{2}}+4\pi r.
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ -\frac{256\pi }{{r}^{2}}+4\pi r & =0 \\ 4\pi r & =\frac{256\pi }{{r}^{2}} \\ 4\pi {r}^{3} & =256\pi  \\ {r}^{3} & =64 \\ r & =\sqrt[3]{64} \\  & =4\,\text{ft}\end{aligned}
$$

Using a calculator, we can verify that if $r<4$ then ${S}^{′}(r)<0,$ and if $r>4$ then ${S}^{′}(r)>0,$ which means that the stationary point $r=4$ is indeed a minimum of $S(r).$

Finally, to find the smallest surface area, we substitute $r=4\,\text{ft}$ into the equation for the surface area $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}S(4) & =\frac{256\pi }{4}+2\pi (4)^{2} \\  & =301.592… \\  & ≈302\,{\text{ft}}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

Therefore, the smallest possible surface area of the cylinder is $S=302\,{\text{ft}}^{2}.$
